description: The Wolfram Language is fundamentally a functional language: functions are ordinary expressions, pure functions are written inline with Function or #/&, and iteration is normally expressed with Map, Fold and Nest rather than loops. This category covers those higher-order operators, the scoping constructs Module/Block/With, and the procedural control-flow statements that remain available when they are the clearest choice.

tools.name: Map
tools.description: Applies a function to each element of an expression, returning a new expression of the same shape. The infix form f /@ expr is the most common way to write it, and a level specification maps at deeper levels of a nested structure. Map works on any expression, not only lists, so f /@ (a + b) gives f[a] + f[b].
tools.usage:
Map[f, expr]
f /@ expr
Map[f, expr, levelspec]
Map[f][expr]

parameters.name: f
parameters.description: Function applied to each part; usually a pure function such as (#^2 &).

parameters.name: levelspec
parameters.description: Levels at which to map, e.g. {2} for level 2 only or {0, Infinity} for every subexpression.

tools.example:
Map[f, {a, b, c}]
#^2 & /@ Range[5]
Map[f, {{1, 2}, {3, 4}}, {2}]
Map[StringLength][{"ab", "cde"}]
tools.notes: Many built-in functions have the Listable attribute and thread automatically, so Sqrt[list] already works without Map. Use MapThread for several lists in parallel and AssociationMap to build key->value pairs.

tools.name: Apply
tools.description: Replaces the head of an expression with a new function, written infix as f @@ expr. Apply[f, {a, b, c}] gives f[a, b, c], which is how you feed a list of values into a function expecting separate arguments. Apply[f, expr, {1}] (written f @@@ expr) applies f at level 1, turning a list of lists into a list of function calls.
tools.usage:
Apply[f, expr]
f @@ expr
Apply[f, expr, levelspec]
f @@@ expr
tools.notes: Plus @@ list and Times @@ list are classic idioms, although Total and Product are clearer and faster for numeric data. f @@@ expr is shorthand for Apply[f, expr, {1}].

tools.name: MapThread
tools.description: Applies a function to corresponding elements of several lists at once, so MapThread[f, {{a1, a2}, {b1, b2}}] gives {f[a1, b1], f[a2, b2]}. All the lists must have the same length. A level specification threads at a deeper level, which is useful for matrices.
tools.usage:
MapThread[f, {list1, list2, ...}]
MapThread[f, {list1, ...}, n]
tools.notes: Equivalent to Apply[f, Transpose[{l1, l2}], {1}] but clearer. For a function that is already Listable, plain arithmetic on the lists is faster.

tools.name: MapIndexed
tools.description: Like Map, but passes each element together with its position, given as an index list such as {3}. This is the idiomatic way to write a loop that needs the running index without a separate counter. A level specification and the option Heads work as in Map.
tools.usage:
MapIndexed[f, expr]
MapIndexed[f, expr, levelspec]
tools.example:
MapIndexed[f, {a, b, c}]
MapIndexed[#1 -> First[#2] &, {"x", "y", "z"}]
MapIndexed[{First[#2], #1} &, {10, 20, 30}]
tools.notes: The index is always a list, so use First[#2] or #2[[1]] to get a plain integer. For two-dimensional data the index is {i, j} at level 2.

tools.name: MapAt
tools.description: Applies a function only to the parts at specified positions, leaving everything else untouched. Positions use the index-list form produced by Position, so MapAt composes naturally with a search. It is the surgical alternative to mapping over a whole structure.
tools.usage:
MapAt[f, expr, n]
MapAt[f, expr, {i, j}]
MapAt[f, expr, {{p1}, {p2}}]
MapAt[f, pos][expr]

tools.name: Scan
tools.description: Evaluates a function on each element of an expression for its side effects and returns Null. Use it when you want Map's traversal but not its result list, for example when printing, sowing or writing to a stream. A Return inside the scanned function exits Scan early, which makes it a controllable iteration construct.
tools.usage:
Scan[f, expr]
Scan[f, expr, levelspec]
tools.example:
Scan[Print, {a, b, c}]
Scan[If[# > 3, Return[#]] &, {1, 5, 2}]
Scan[Export["out" <> ToString[#] <> ".txt", #] &, data]
tools.notes: Scan avoids building an intermediate list, so it uses less memory than Map when only side effects matter.

tools.name: Fold
tools.description: Combines the elements of a list left to right with a binary function, carrying an accumulator. Fold[f, x, {a, b, c}] gives f[f[f[x, a], b], c], and the two-argument form Fold[f, list] uses the first element as the starting value. Fold is the general replacement for an accumulation loop and is the basis of running totals, parsers and state machines.
tools.usage:
Fold[f, x, list]
Fold[f, list]
Fold[f][list]

parameters.name: f
parameters.description: Binary function f[accumulator, element] returning the new accumulator.

tools.notes: Use FoldList when you need every intermediate value. Accumulate is a fast special case of FoldList[Plus, ...].

tools.name: FoldList
tools.description: Like Fold, but returns the list of every intermediate accumulator value including the starting one. FoldList[f, x, {a, b}] gives {x, f[x, a], f[f[x, a], b]}. This is the tool for running totals, cumulative products, random walks and any trace of an iterative process.
tools.usage:
FoldList[f, x, list]
FoldList[f, list]
tools.example:
FoldList[Plus, 0, {1, 2, 3}]
FoldList[Times, {1, 2, 3, 4}]
FoldList[#1 + #2 &, 0, RandomChoice[{-1, 1}, 10]]
tools.notes: Accumulate[list] is a much faster equivalent of Rest[FoldList[Plus, 0, list]] for numeric data.

tools.name: Nest
tools.description: Applies a function to an expression a fixed number of times and returns only the final result, so Nest[f, x, 3] gives f[f[f[x]]]. It expresses fixed-count iteration without a loop variable and works with any expression, symbolic or numeric. Use it for iterated maps, repeated refinement and simple dynamical systems.
tools.usage: Nest[f, expr, n]
tools.notes: Nest evaluates f exactly n times; if the result stops changing, FixedPoint is a better fit because it detects convergence.

tools.name: NestList
tools.description: Gives the list of results of applying a function 0 through n times, starting with the original expression. NestList[f, x, 3] returns {x, f[x], f[f[x]], f[f[f[x]]]}, which is exactly the trajectory of an iterated map. It is the standard way to generate orbits, sequences and time series from a recurrence.
tools.usage: NestList[f, expr, n]
tools.example:
NestList[f, x, 3]
NestList[2 # &, 1, 10]
ListPlot[NestList[3.9 # (1 - #) &, 0.2, 100]]
tools.notes: For sequences defined by a recurrence in closed form, RecurrenceTable or RSolve may be faster and exact.

tools.name: NestWhile
tools.description: Repeatedly applies a function while a test on the current result remains True, returning the first value that fails the test. Extra arguments let the test see the last m results, add a maximum iteration count, and shift which result is returned. This is the functional equivalent of a while loop.
tools.usage:
NestWhile[f, expr, test]
NestWhile[f, expr, test, m]
NestWhile[f, expr, test, m, max]
NestWhile[f, expr, test, m, max, n]

parameters.name: test
parameters.description: Predicate applied to the most recent result (or last m results) to decide whether to continue.

parameters.name: m
parameters.description: Number of most recent results supplied to the test; All supplies every result so far.

parameters.name: max
parameters.description: Maximum number of applications of f.

tools.example:
NestWhile[# / 2 &, 1024, EvenQ]
NestWhile[Floor[#/2] &, 100, # > 1 &]
NestWhile[f, x, UnsameQ, 2]
NestWhile[# + 1 &, 0, # < 10 &, 1, 100]
tools.notes: NestWhile[f, x, UnsameQ, 2] is the idiom for iterating until the value stops changing, which is what FixedPoint does directly.

tools.name: NestWhileList
tools.description: Like NestWhile but returns the complete list of values produced, including the final one that fails the test. Use it to record the whole path of a convergent iteration, for plotting or diagnostics. It takes the same optional arguments as NestWhile.
tools.usage:
NestWhileList[f, expr, test]
NestWhileList[f, expr, test, m, max]
tools.example:
NestWhileList[# / 2 &, 64, EvenQ]
NestWhileList[If[EvenQ[#], #/2, 3 # + 1] &, 27, # > 1 &]

tools.name: FixedPoint
tools.description: Applies a function repeatedly until the result no longer changes, then returns that fixed point. An optional maximum iteration count guards against non-convergence, and the SameTest option lets you accept approximate convergence for floating-point work. It is the natural expression of 'iterate until stable'.
tools.usage:
FixedPoint[f, expr]
FixedPoint[f, expr, n]
FixedPoint[f, expr, SameTest -> test]
tools.example:
FixedPoint[Cos, 1.0]
FixedPoint[(# + 2 / #) / 2 &, 1.0]
FixedPoint[# /. {a -> b, b -> c} &, a]
FixedPoint[N[Cos[#]] &, 1.0, SameTest -> (Abs[#1 - #2] < 10^-6 &)]
tools.notes: Without a count or SameTest, a non-converging function loops until interrupted or until $IterationLimit is hit. ReplaceRepeated (//.) is the rule-based analogue.

tools.name: FixedPointList
tools.description: Returns the full list of successive values produced while iterating to a fixed point, ending with two equal values. Length[FixedPointList[...]] - 2 therefore counts the iterations needed, making it useful for convergence studies. It accepts the same count and SameTest arguments as FixedPoint.
tools.usage:
FixedPointList[f, expr]
FixedPointList[f, expr, n]
tools.example:
FixedPointList[Cos, 1.0]
Length[FixedPointList[(# + 2/#)/2 &, 1.0]]
FixedPointList[N[Cos[#]] &, 1.0, 5]

tools.name: Function
tools.description: Creates a pure (anonymous) function. Function[x, body] names its parameter explicitly, Function[{x, y}, body] takes several, and the short form body & uses the positional slots #, #1, #2 and ##. Pure functions are ordinary expressions that can be stored, passed and composed, and Function has attribute HoldAll so the body is not evaluated until the function is applied.
tools.usage:
Function[body]
Function[x, body]
Function[{x, y, ...}, body]
body &
Function[{x}, body, attrs]
tools.example:
Function[x, x^2][5]
#^2 & [5]
Function[{x, y}, x + y][2, 3]
(#1 + #2 &) @@ {2, 3}
Map[Function[t, t / Total[data]], data]
tools.notes: Named parameters (Function[x, ...]) are safer than slots when functions are nested, because inner # refers to the innermost &. Function[{x}, body, HoldAll] makes a pure function that holds its arguments.

tools.name: Slot
tools.description: Represents an argument inside a short-form pure function: # (or #1) is the first argument, #2 the second, and #name picks a named key out of an Association argument. SlotSequence (## and ##2) stands for all arguments from a given position onward. Slots are only meaningful inside a & function.
tools.usage:
#
#n
#name
##
##n
tools.notes: In nested & functions the inner # shadows the outer one; use Function[x, ...] with named variables to avoid confusion.

tools.name: Composition
tools.description: Builds the composition of functions, so Composition[f, g, h][x] gives f[g[h[x]]]. The result is itself a function that can be stored and mapped. Composition applies its arguments right to left, matching mathematical notation.
tools.usage:
Composition[f, g, ...]
Composition[f, g][x]
f @* g
tools.example:
Composition[f, g, h][x]
Composition[Sqrt, Abs][-9]
(Sqrt @* Abs)[-16]
Map[Total @* Range, {3, 4, 5}]
tools.notes: The infix operator @* is shorthand for Composition. Composition automatically drops Identity and flattens nested compositions.

tools.name: RightComposition
tools.description: Composes functions in left-to-right order, so RightComposition[f, g][x] gives g[f[x]]. Written infix as /*, it reads like a pipeline and pairs naturally with the operator forms of Select, Map and SortBy. Use it when the data-flow order is clearer than mathematical composition order.
tools.usage:
RightComposition[f, g, ...]
f /* g /* h
tools.example:
RightComposition[f, g][x]
(Range /* Total)[5]
pipeline = Select[EvenQ] /* Map[#^2 &] /* Total;
pipeline[Range[10]]

tools.name: Identity
tools.description: Returns its argument unchanged. It is used as a neutral default for function-valued options and arguments, and as a placeholder in compositions and Through. Identity[x] evaluates to x immediately.
tools.usage: Identity[expr]
tools.example:
Identity[x + y]
Map[Identity, {1, 2, 3}]
f[x_, g_: Identity] := g[x^2];
f[3]
f[3, Sqrt]

tools.name: Through
tools.description: Distributes an argument list across a collection of functions: Through[(f + g)[x]] gives f[x] + g[x], and Through[{f, g}[x]] gives {f[x], g[x]}. It is the standard way to apply several functions to the same input and keep the enclosing structure. An optional second argument restricts which head is threaded.
tools.usage:
Through[p[x]]
Through[p[x], h]
tools.example:
Through[{Min, Max, Mean}[{3, 1, 4, 1, 5}]]
Through[(f + g)[x]]
Through[{Sin, Cos}[Pi/4]]
tools.notes: Through[{f, g}[x]] is a compact alternative to writing #[x] & /@ {f, g}.

tools.name: Operate
tools.description: Applies a function to the head of an expression rather than to its arguments: Operate[p, f[x, y]] gives p[f][x, y]. With a level argument it reaches deeper into curried heads. It is the tool for transforming or wrapping the operator part of an expression.
tools.usage:
Operate[p, expr]
Operate[p, expr, n]
tools.example:
Operate[p, f[x, y]]
Operate[Composition[g], f[x]]
Operate[p, f[x][y], 2]
tools.notes: Compare MapAt[p, expr, 0] which replaces the head with p[head] only at level 0, and Head which merely reads it.

tools.name: Outer
tools.description: Forms the generalized outer product, applying a function to every combination of elements from the supplied lists. Outer[Times, u, v] gives the usual outer product matrix, while Outer[f, l1, l2] gives a matrix of f[a, b] values. Level specifications let you take outer products of matrices and higher tensors.
tools.usage:
Outer[f, list1, list2, ...]
Outer[f, list1, list2, n]
tools.example:
Outer[Times, {1, 2}, {3, 4, 5}]
Outer[f, {a, b}, {x, y}]
Outer[List, {1, 2}, {3, 4}]
Outer[Times, IdentityMatrix[2], IdentityMatrix[2]] // Dimensions
tools.notes: Outer keeps the nested array structure, whereas Tuples flattens the combinations into a list of tuples. KroneckerProduct is the matrix-shaped version of Outer[Times, ...].

tools.name: Inner
tools.description: The generalized inner product: Inner[f, u, v, g] combines corresponding elements with f and reduces them with g, so Inner[Times, u, v, Plus] is the ordinary dot product. Replacing f and g with other operations gives max-plus algebras, boolean matrix products and similar constructions. It works on vectors, matrices and higher tensors.
tools.usage:
Inner[f, list1, list2, g]
Inner[f, list1, list2]
tools.example:
Inner[Times, {a, b}, {x, y}, Plus]
Inner[Plus, {1, 2, 3}, {10, 20, 30}, Min]
Inner[And, {True, False}, {True, True}, Or]
tools.notes: For plain numeric dot products, Dot (.) is far faster because it uses optimized BLAS routines.

tools.name: Thread
tools.description: Threads a function over lists that appear as its arguments, so Thread[f[{a, b}, x]] gives {f[a, x], f[b, x]}. This is exactly what the Listable attribute does automatically for built-in functions. Thread[{k1, k2} -> {v1, v2}] is the standard idiom for building a list of replacement rules.
tools.usage:
Thread[f[args]]
Thread[f[args], h]
Thread[f[args], h, n]
tools.example:
Thread[f[{a, b, c}]]
Thread[{x, y, z} -> {1, 2, 3}]
Thread[f[{1, 2}, x]]
Thread[Equal[{x, y}, {1, 2}]]
tools.notes: Thread[lhs -> rhs] requires the two lists to have equal length. AssociationThread builds an Association from the same kind of key/value pair.

tools.name: Do
tools.description: Evaluates an expression repeatedly for its side effects, using the same iterator syntax as Table and Sum, and returns Null. Use it for loops whose purpose is assignment, printing or file writing rather than producing a list. Do has attribute HoldAll, and Break, Continue and Return work inside it.
tools.usage:
Do[expr, n]
Do[expr, {i, imax}]
Do[expr, {i, imin, imax, di}]
Do[expr, {i, ...}, {j, ...}]
tools.example:
Do[Print[i], {i, 3}]
s = 0; Do[s += i^2, {i, 10}]; s
Do[Print[{i, j}], {i, 2}, {j, 2}]
Do[If[PrimeQ[k], Print[k]; Break[]], {k, 10, 20}]
tools.notes: Prefer Table, Map or Fold when you want a result; Do is for side effects. Sow/Reap collects values from inside a Do without an explicit accumulator.

tools.name: While
tools.description: Repeatedly evaluates a body while a test evaluates to True, returning Null. Both arguments are held, so the test is re-evaluated each pass and normally involves variables updated in the body. Break[] exits early and Continue[] skips to the next iteration.
tools.usage:
While[test, body]
While[test]
tools.example:
i = 1; While[i < 5, Print[i]; i++]
x = 100; While[x > 1, x = x/2]; x
n = 0; While[True, n++; If[n > 10, Break[]]]; n
tools.notes: The loop stops if the test gives anything other than True, including an unevaluated symbolic inequality. $IterationLimit aborts runaway loops.

tools.name: For
tools.description: A C-style loop taking a start expression, a test, an increment and a body, all held unevaluated. For[i = 1, i <= n, i++, body] is the familiar counted loop. It exists for readability when porting procedural code; Do and Table are usually more idiomatic and faster in Wolfram Language.
tools.usage:
For[start, test, incr, body]
For[start, test, incr]
tools.example:
For[i = 1, i <= 3, i++, Print[i]]
For[{i = 1, s = 0}, i <= 10, i++, s += i]; s
For[i = 10, i > 0, i -= 3, Print[i]]
tools.notes: Note the comma-separated arguments (not semicolons as in C) and that the body is optional. Break[] and Continue[] work as expected.

tools.name: If
tools.description: Evaluates one branch or another depending on a condition. If[test, t] returns Null when the test is False, If[test, t, f] supplies the false branch, and a fourth argument handles the case where the test is neither True nor False. Only the selected branch is evaluated because If has attribute HoldRest.
tools.usage:
If[test, then]
If[test, then, else]
If[test, then, else, unknown]
tools.example:
If[3 > 2, "yes", "no"]
f[x_] := If[x >= 0, Sqrt[x], I Sqrt[-x]]
If[x > 0, 1, -1, Indeterminate]
If[FileExistsQ["data.csv"], Import["data.csv"], {}]
tools.notes: A symbolic condition returns the unevaluated If unless a fourth argument is given; use TrueQ to force a definite boolean, and Piecewise for functions defined by cases in symbolic mathematics.

tools.name: Which
tools.description: Evaluates test/value pairs in order and returns the value for the first test that is True. Which[t1, v1, t2, v2, True, default] is the idiomatic multi-way branch with a catch-all. Tests are evaluated lazily from left to right and only the selected value is evaluated.
tools.usage: Which[test1, value1, test2, value2, ...]
tools.notes: If no test is True the result is Null. Use True as the final test to supply a default, and Piecewise when the result must stay symbolic for calculus.

tools.name: Switch
tools.description: Compares an expression against a sequence of patterns and returns the value paired with the first pattern that matches. Unlike Which it dispatches on the form of a value rather than on boolean tests, and the patterns may use blanks, alternatives and conditions. The pattern _ serves as the default case.
tools.usage: Switch[expr, form1, value1, form2, value2, ...]
tools.example:
Switch[3, 1, "one", 2, "two", _, "many"]
Switch[x, _Integer, "int", _Real, "real", _String, "string", _, "other"] /. x -> 2.5
Switch[cmd, "start" | "go", run[], "stop", halt[], _, Message[cmd::unknown]]
tools.notes: Switch returns Null and leaves the expression unevaluated if nothing matches, so always include a trailing _ case.

tools.name: Module
tools.description: Creates lexically scoped local variables by renaming them to unique symbols such as x$123 during evaluation. It is the default scoping construct for function bodies that need temporary variables, and initial values may be given as x = val. Module has attribute HoldAll, so the body is not evaluated until the locals are created.
tools.usage:
Module[{x, y, ...}, body]
Module[{x = x0, y = y0}, body]
tools.example:
f[n_] := Module[{s = 0}, Do[s += i, {i, n}]; s]
f[10]
Module[{x}, x = 5; x^2]
g[list_] := Module[{sorted = Sort[list], n = Length[list]}, sorted[[Ceiling[n/2]]]]
tools.notes: Use Module for temporary variables, With for constants that should be substituted before evaluation, and Block for temporarily overriding the value of a global symbol.

tools.name: Block
tools.description: Creates dynamically scoped local values: the listed symbols keep their names but their global values are saved, cleared and restored when the block exits. This is how you temporarily change system variables such as $RecursionLimit or a symbol that appears inside already-defined expressions. Numeric functions like NIntegrate use Block internally for their iteration variables.
tools.usage:
Block[{x, y, ...}, body]
Block[{x = x0, ...}, body]
tools.example:
x = 10;
Block[{x = 2}, x^3]
x
Block[{$RecursionLimit = 10000}, deepRecursion[5000]]
Block[{$MaxExtraPrecision = 1000}, N[expr, 50]]
tools.notes: Because the symbol name is unchanged, Block affects every expression referring to that symbol anywhere, including inside other functions. Prefer Module unless you specifically need that behaviour.

tools.name: With
tools.description: Substitutes constant values into an expression before evaluating it, like a let-binding. With[{x = a}, body] literally replaces x by a throughout body, which makes it the right way to inject values into held expressions such as Manipulate, Hold or delayed definitions. Later bindings in the same With cannot refer to earlier ones; nest two With blocks for that.
tools.usage: With[{x = x0, y = y0, ...}, body]
tools.example:
With[{n = 5}, n^2]
With[{f = Sin}, Plot[f[x], {x, 0, Pi}]]
With[{v = computeOnce[]}, Hold[g[v]]]
With[{a = 2}, With[{b = a + 1}, a * b]]
tools.notes: With is the standard fix for values not being captured inside Hold, DynamicModule or a SetDelayed right-hand side.

tools.name: Return
tools.description: Immediately returns a value from the enclosing function body, Do, While, For or Scan. Return[] returns Null. In Wolfram Language most functions simply evaluate to the value of their last expression, so Return is mainly used for early exit from a procedural loop or a guard clause.
tools.usage:
Return[expr]
Return[]
tools.example:
f[x_] := Module[{}, If[x < 0, Return["negative"]]; Sqrt[x]]
f[-1]
Scan[If[# > 3, Return[#]] &, {1, 2, 5, 7}]
tools.notes: Return only escapes the innermost scoping or loop construct, which surprises people coming from other languages; Throw/Catch gives reliable non-local exit.

tools.name: Throw
tools.description: Aborts evaluation and hands a value to the nearest enclosing Catch. Throw[value, tag] attaches a tag so that only a Catch with a matching tag pattern intercepts it. Together with Catch it provides reliable non-local exit from arbitrarily deep recursion, mapping or iteration.
tools.usage:
Throw[value]
Throw[value, tag]
tools.example:
Catch[Do[If[i^2 > 50, Throw[i]], {i, 100}]]
Catch[Throw[bad, "err"], "err"]
Catch[Scan[If[# < 0, Throw[#, neg]] &, {3, 1, -2}], neg]
tools.notes: An uncaught Throw produces a Throw::nocatch message and leaves the expression unevaluated. Tags are matched as patterns, so _ catches everything.

tools.name: Catch
tools.description: Evaluates an expression and returns the value of the first matching Throw that occurs inside it, or the expression's own value if nothing is thrown. Catch[expr, form] only intercepts throws whose tag matches the given pattern, and a third argument applies a function to the thrown value and tag. It is the standard mechanism for early exit and lightweight exception handling.
tools.usage:
Catch[expr]
Catch[expr, form]
Catch[expr, form, f]
tools.example:
Catch[Map[If[# < 0, Throw["negative found"], Sqrt[#]] &, {1, 4, -9}]]
Catch[Throw[7, tag], _, {#2, #1} &]
find[list_] := Catch[Scan[If[PrimeQ[#], Throw[#]] &, list]; None]
find[{4, 6, 7, 8}]
tools.notes: Catch and Throw are dynamically scoped, so the Throw can be anywhere in the evaluation, including inside a called function. Use distinct tags to avoid intercepting throws from library code.

tools.name: Sow
tools.description: Records a value for later collection by an enclosing Reap, optionally under one or more tags. It lets a deeply nested computation emit intermediate results without threading an accumulator through every function. Sow returns its own argument, so it can be inserted into an existing expression without changing the result.
tools.usage:
Sow[e]
Sow[e, tag]
Sow[e, {tag1, tag2, ...}]
tools.example:
Reap[Do[If[PrimeQ[i], Sow[i]], {i, 20}]]
Reap[Sum[Sow[k^2], {k, 4}]]
Reap[Do[Sow[i, If[EvenQ[i], even, odd]], {i, 6}], _, Rule]
tools.notes: Sow/Reap is the fast, idiomatic replacement for AppendTo in a loop, since it avoids repeated list copying.

tools.name: Reap
tools.description: Evaluates an expression and returns {value, sownLists} where sownLists collects everything Sow recorded during the evaluation. A pattern argument selects which tags to reap, and a function argument combines each tag with its list of values. This pair is the standard way to gather results from inside loops, recursion or visitor-style traversals.
tools.usage:
Reap[expr]
Reap[expr, patt]
Reap[expr, patt, f]
tools.example:
Reap[Do[Sow[i^2], {i, 5}]]
Last[Reap[Do[If[PrimeQ[i], Sow[i]], {i, 30}]]][[1]]
Reap[Sow[1, a]; Sow[2, b]; Sow[3, a], _, Rule]
tools.notes: When nothing is sown the second element is {}, so wrap with Flatten or use a default. Nested Reaps only catch the tags they match, which lets libraries use private tags safely.
